title: Supervision 6 essay
description: What is the evidence that the kidneys produce urine by a process of ultrafiltration, followed by fluid reabsorption, involving expenditure by the tubule cells?
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 6. Write it here, the same way you’ll write your essays in the online exam.

  • Planning. Plan your essay before you start writing, on paper if you like.
  • Equations. Type simple ones into your text, as you’d write them by hand (× is among the special characters, under Ω). For one with a fraction, use the formula tool, Σ. Say what each equation means, and then use it.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your work.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your work, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Saving. Your work is saved in this browser as you type, so you can stop and come back to it. It stays here until you submit it.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the ✓ tile at the bottom right), check your work and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: The evidence for filtration and reabsorption
questions.text:
What is the evidence that the kidneys produce urine by a process of ultrafiltration, followed by fluid reabsorption, involving expenditure by the tubule cells?

Write in continuous prose, with an introduction, paragraphs that each make one point, and a conclusion. Support your argument with mechanisms, evidence and numbers from the lectures.
questions.guidance:
Read this after you’ve written your essay, and use it before the supervision to look back over what you wrote. It isn’t a model essay. It sets out the ground a good answer covers.

What the title asks. Evidence for three claims: urine starts as an ultrafiltrate of plasma; most of the filtrate is then reabsorbed; and reabsorption costs the tubule cells energy. It doesn’t ask how the kidney works, but how we know. The long dispute between filtration and secretion gives the essay a natural shape: Bowman (1842) thought the glomeruli secreted water, while Ludwig (1844) saw that urine formation depends on arterial pressure and proposed filtration.

  • Filtration: the early, indirect evidence. Heidenhain (1874) found that indigo carmine coloured the tubules, not the glomeruli, and concluded that urine was secreted; von Sobieranski (1895) saw that the dye could be concentrated in the tubules as water was reabsorbed, and Bieter and Hirschfelder (1924) found it concentrated only in tubules whose glomeruli had a circulation. Cullis (1906) found that a substance reached the urine if it reached the glomeruli through the renal artery, but not if it reached the tubules through the renal portal vein. Say what each result rules out, and why it isn’t conclusive alone.
  • Filtration: the direct evidence. Wearn and Richards (1924) collected fluid from Bowman’s capsule in frogs by micropuncture: it was free of protein, it held glucose (when the frog had been given glucose) that the bladder urine didn’t, its Cl− was higher than the urine’s, and it stopped entering the pipette when the blood flow stopped. The capsular fluid is plasma without its protein, and its formation depends on the blood’s pressure. The Starling forces explain it: a glomerular capillary pressure of about 60 mmHg against about 15 in the capsule and an oncotic pressure rising from 21 to 33 along the capillary, so the net pressure favours filtration all along it (GFR = Kf × net pressure). The structure of the barrier (fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes and their slit diaphragms) explains why protein is held back.
  • Reabsorption: its scale. The urea argument: about 0.5 mol of urea is excreted a day at a plasma concentration of 7 mM, so at least 70 L of plasma must be filtered a day, but less than 2 L of urine is made (an underestimate, because some urea is reabsorbed). Inulin, freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, gives a GFR of 125 mL/min (180 L a day) against a urine flow of about 1 mL/min: over 99% of the filtered water is reabsorbed. Glucose has a clearance of zero below its threshold, although it’s filtered. Ribbert (1883): removing the medulla raised urine volume two- to three-fold.
  • Reabsorption: where, and how. Richards and Walker (1937) sampled the tubules by micropuncture: the osmotic pressure and Cl− are lower in distal than in proximal fluid, and glucose falls along the proximal tubule, but rises when phlorhizin blocks its reabsorption, because water is still being reabsorbed. The concentration of inulin rises about three-fold along the proximal tubule while the fluid stays isosmotic with plasma: about two-thirds of the filtrate, water and solute together, is reabsorbed there. In split-oil-drop experiments (Windhager and colleagues, 1959, in Necturus) the inulin in a column of fluid held in a tubule rises with time, and fluid reabsorption depends on the Na+ in the column. Hirokawa (1908) and the freezing-point studies of Wirz and colleagues (1951) show the medulla’s osmotic pressure rising towards the papilla and following the urine’s.
  • Expenditure by the tubule cells. Reabsorption runs against gradients: glucose falls to almost nothing along the proximal tubule, and the distal fluid becomes hypotonic, so solute is removed without water. Bainbridge (1913) found that perfused frog kidneys made a hypotonic fluid, but an isotonic one after poisoning with mercuric chloride. Schatzmann and colleagues (1958): in stopped-flow perfusions of the proximal tubule, 27% of the fluid was reabsorbed in 20 minutes, but only about 10% with 2,4-dinitrophenol or ouabain, so fluid reabsorption depends on metabolism and on the Na+/K+-ATPase. Transport maxima (glucose 375 mg/min) show saturable carriers. The kidney’s O2 consumption rises with the Na+ it reabsorbs, and its cells (proximal tubule, thick ascending limb) are packed with mitochondria.
  • The limits of the evidence. Much of the early work was on amphibians, and was later confirmed by micropuncture in mammals. Filtration itself costs the tubule nothing: the heart provides the pressure. And filtration followed by reabsorption isn’t the whole story: the tubules secrete too (PAH, H+, K+), which the best essays mention.

What makes an essay stand out. Every piece of evidence is tied to one of the three claims, and its inference is spelt out. The numbers are there (125 mL/min, over 99%, 27% against 10%). Direct and indirect evidence are told apart, and so are frogs and mammals. And the conclusion says how strong the case is for each claim.
